Original: http://www.webdevguides.co.uk/xslt/add-html-xhtml-doctype-to-xslt-style-sheet

XSLT (eXtensible Stylesheet Language Transformations) allows you to style XML documents by transforming them to another format such as HTML. By doing this you can style an XML document easily with CSS.

However, in order for the document to render correctly in many browsers, you will need to use the same DOCTYPE as you would in a normal HTML page. Fortunately this can be added easily to a XSLT document.

Firstly, locate the xsl:output tag which looks like this:

<xsl:output method="html" version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" indent="yes">

For an XHTML 1.1 Strict doctype, which in a HTML document is as follows:

<!DOCTYPE html PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD XHTML 1.1//EN"
 "http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml11/DTD/xhtml11.dtd">

You add it to an XSLT document by simply taking the two quoted parts of the doctype and add them to the doctype-public and doctype-system attributes:

<xsl:output method="html" version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" indent="yes"
 doctype-public="-//W3C//DTD XHTML 1.1//EN"
 doctype-system="http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml11/DTD/xhtml11.dtd"/>

The same method works for any XHTML or HTML doctype, apart from HTML 5.

Indeed HTML 5 is a fiddly beast when it comes to XSLT; for example see How to output with XSLT on Stack Overflow. There are two methods that are available, which may not necessarily work on all browsers: the recommended one is to use this xsl:output tag:

<xsl:output method="html" doctype-system="about:legacy-compat"/>

However this may leave “http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml1/DTD/xhtml1-transitional.dtd” in the doctype.

The other alternative is to have it output the doctype directly:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<xsl:stylesheet version="1.0" xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
 <xsl:output method="html" encoding="utf-8" indent="yes" />
 <xsl:template match="/">
 <xsl:text disable-output-escaping='yes'><!DOCTYPE html></xsl:text>
 <!--HTML Template code here-->
 </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

However some browsers and XSLT processors do not support this.

Remember also that all HTML code must be valid XML; unlike HTML, XML doesn’t allow non-closed elements (like “<br>”; it must be “<br/>” instead).

What is the physiological benefit of a traditional funeral?

I have a bit of a different take on this.

I think the grieving process should be based around the persons life, not their death parade. I've been to two funerals in my life... one where we were sad and formal. The other where we were... celebratory. Both had tears, both were incredibly sad. But in the former, we came out with a sense of foreboding, of a view of our own mortality and negativity. When we celebrated a life with a bit of beer and a planting of a tree, a life giver, we felt like we were grieving but moving on. We were doing something that meant we could move to better things in our lives, and while we still had a fear of our mortality, it was that we should be trying to make the most of it, not overly protect ourselves.

Grieving is required over these times, but they way you position that grief is going to be an indicator of how you come out of it all.

Also, I feel like more positive funerals are required in this day and age. I want to be cremated in a sturdy cardboard box that people get to write and draw all over in marker. They can crack a couple of jokes at my expense, and fuck, I'll make sure they have a good bar tab as well. I want people to look back and think "Hey, that ViolentMasticator was pretty awesome through her life, I'm glad we could send her off in a way that represented that"

I've been to a few funerals too many. I've experienced both of the environments you describe. It's not a bad thing to have a quiet funeral. It often comes down to the culture of the person who died.

In some cultures, you celebrate their life.

In others, you're saying your last goodbye.

Oh of course. Hence why it should be about that persons life. The funeral of my mother will be much different to the funeral of my father. But funerals are often when people need to talk and console each other. Quiet reverence should be when you are solitary, not surrounded by the people who could comfort you.
I've never been to a quiet wake where people aren't consoling each other.

I'm in IT so this is just my point of view with no formal psychology background to back it.

We don't really talk about death. We talk about how we loved this cake, or found that dress ugly, or how we would be offended by something, we even talk about a disease we had or have but we tend to avoid talking about our death or the death of someone we love. And when death is a conversation subject, it usually is a philosophical talk about the concept.

Funerals serve as reality check, it makes that death real and makes you have to deal with it. It also brings all the friends and family together so that the one who suffered the loss doesn't have to go through it alone. In some cases it also serves as a way to honor someones life and deeds which serves as a comfort for the ones left behind, it lends a certain sense of pride to balance all the grief. For those who are religious (I am not) it is a way of fulfilling all the right rituals that will assure that the dead person will have access to the best afterlife their religion allows. In these cases I find that the grief is there but funerals have a sense of purpose to them. We have to do this and that or else this and that won't happen. So it kind of makes the grief take a second place because the dead person is "going to a better place" and it brings people comfort to know they did all they could and should to insure that everlasting bliss.

I could go on but this has already turned into a TL; DR; :)
Nothing, once the blood has stopped pumping no funeral traditional or otherwise will recirculate a deadman's blood.
Well, physiologically, I suppose a "traditional" funeral would trumph a cremation. Not much physiology left after that.

After volunteering with a couple hospice companies and attending way to many funerals, memorials, wakes, and grave side services then I can remember, I've become a connoisseur of funerals. The ones to avoid are led by priests, reverends, or worst of all lay priests (like Deacons or Mormons). Funeral Directors usually put on a pretty good show (efficient timing and appropriate focus on the dead person's life and loves), but are usually way over priced. The best services usually have upbeat yet thematically appropriate music; amazing food; one or two inspirational talks, stories, or poems of no more than 3 minutes a piece; a brief life sketch of the dead; and physical activity of some kind (like a short walk through the sun shine, memorial 5K fun run, or motor cycle and ATV race). Seriously, Biker and Redneck memorial services are the shit.

I recommend cremation, which will usually be the cheapest option and the dead won't care anyway. Some of my fondest memories are of the inadvertent screw ups that destroyed the artificial solemness that old fools try to impose on the process. Like the time an old Irish woman passed. Everyone was standing around drinking quietly, talking about the lady, and few of them had really even known her. All of the sudden, the lady's great granddaughter (probably 4 or 5 years old) started attaching My Little Pony stickers to the lady's casket and coloring on it with crayon. Not a care in the world, just started decorating the casket, because she had nothing better to do. All the old people were scandalized, the girls parents and relatives were horrified- while me, the other hospice volunteers, and the funeral home's staff were desperate to not bust up laughing. That little girl made our week.
A traditional funeral usually employs six pall bearers to carry the casket, so I guess that physiologically six guys get their reps in for the day.
yeah depending on the mass of the coffin and the body inside I'd also recommend a few lunges along the way

I'd strongly suggest pursuing a so-called natural burial.

It's a good read and pretty clearly indicates that funerals better serve loved ones than the deceased themselves.
